newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Smiling, Boutros-Ghali bids farewell to U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: Smiling, Boutros-Ghali bids farewell to U.N. post.

text.p: As several hundred staff members clapped, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali left the United Nations complex on Tuesday, ending a turbulent five years as the world's top diplomat.

"Thank you for everything you have done. I wish you a happy New Year. I wish success for the United Nations. I wish success for my successor Kofi Annan," he said, in reference to the 58-year old Ghanaian head of peacekeeping who takes over as secretary-general for a five year-term on Tuesday.

Boutros-Ghali, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister and architect of the Camp David talks that led to the 1979 peace treaty between Israel and Egypt, said he would offer his "modest" services to work for peace in the Middle East but he did not specify how.
"I have worked to achieve this peace since 1966 and I am ready to continue contributing in a more modest way to peace bulding in the Middle East," he said.

Boutros-Ghali, 74, an intellectual law professor and author who assimilated large quantities of information quickly, was jolted in his quest for a second term by a U.S. veto, an event that still puzzled him.
He intends to complete work on a book he wrote over the summer on "Cairo's Road to Jerusalem", expected to be published by Random House in 1997.

He had accompanied the late President Anwar Sadat, murdered in 1981, on his historic trips to Jerusalem that eventually resulted in the peace agreement. For this Boutros-Ghali was castigated in the Arab world for many years as "the academic engineer of Arab surrender."

He will arrive in Cairo on Thursday with a stopover in Paris. After that his spokeswoman, Sylvana Foa, an American, who is also leaving the United Nations, said he would probably return to Paris to reflect and write another book, probably on his five years as secretary-general.

In his comments to reporters throughout the day, Boutros-Ghali also said his biggest accomplishment at the United Nations was maintaining some independence for the world body, a veiled reference to his disputes with Washington.

"I believe that I have tried to maintain a minimum of independence for the United Nations, " he said when asked to discuss his biggest accomplishments and biggest failures. "And I believe that I was not successful to overcome the financial crisis," he added.

The United States blocked his bid for a second term, insisting he had to go because he had not done enough to reform the U.N. bureaucracy and because a tight-fisted Republican Congress would not pay the $1.4 billion U.S. debt to the United Nations while he remained at his helm.

Almost all diplomats in the world body discount the reform argument, saying that despite having 70,000 U.N. peacekeeping troops in the field during his first three years, he did more to trim the bureaucracy than any of his predecessors.

Instead they believe he was doomed because his candidacy overlapped with the U.S. presidential election -- a coincidence that occurs only every 20 years -- and Republicans made him and the United Nations an issue in the campaign.

His aides say that over the last few months he had asked Ambassador Madeleine Albright, the next U.S. secretary of state, why Washington opposed him so strongly. But they said he received only the standard answers on Congress and reform, which he doubted were the real reason.
He fought back publicly in his Dec. 17 final speech to the U.N. General Assembly, the first time he publicly showed any bitterness.
"We know what causes (the U.N. financial crisis) and what is needed to end it. It is not the result of mismanagement. It is the refusal to fulfil a treaty obligation," he said.
"Now that a new secretary-general is being appointed, all arrears should be paid at once, as has been promised so often in the past few months," he said.
He stressed the importance of independence to accomplish any reforms and rebutted Albright's oft-repeated U.S. assertion that a secretary-general's first thoughts in the day should focus on reform.

"Throughout the past five years, the first thing I thought of when I awoke in the morning were my responsibilities as secretary-general to the ideal of the Charter and independence and credibility of the organisation," he said.
